1121.title: Parvati's tapas
1121.hook: Parvati wins Shiva by her own tapas, and refuses to hear him mocked; why Hindus still keep vows and fasts for Shiva
1121.carry: tapas: devotion proven by steady effort
1121.tomorrow: why did Parvati's mother faint at the wedding?
1121.howItsDone: Hindus tell Parvati's tapas and her marriage to Shiva in the Shiva Purana and in poetry; many devotees keep Monday fasts for Shiva, and some women keep fasts in Parvati's honor, such as Hartalika Teej, praying for a good marriage or for their husbands' welfare.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Purana, Kama was burned to ash by the third eye: desire forced from outside couldn't win Shiva.
screen: `KAMA, BURNED TO ASH.` · `A FOURTH SELECTION.`

segments.voice: A princess takes off her jewels. She sets aside her silk and puts on bark. She leaves her father's palace for the mountains, a place where Shiva once sat, and begins. In the Shiva Purana, Parvati has seen what happened to Kama. Beauty didn't win Shiva; help from the gods didn't win him. So she'll do what Shiva himself does. She'll practice tapas. And one day, deep into it, a visitor comes up the path: a young ascetic with matted hair and a staff, who sits down and asks, very politely, what on earth she thinks she's doing.
screen: `JEWELS OFF, BARK ON.` → `SHE'LL DO WHAT SHIVA DOES.` → `A VISITOR COMES UP THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Tapas is austerity, disciplined effort that burns away what's easy and leaves what's strong. In the story, Parvati's tapas grows harder and harder. She stands in the cold, and sits among fires in the heat. She eats less, then less again, and tradition says she gave up even fallen leaves, which is why one of her names is Aparna. Then the visitor. He's courteous at first, then starts in on Shiva. Why this one? He smears himself with ash from cremation grounds. He wears snakes and rides a bull. No house, no family, and he burned the god of love. A woman like you, he says, could marry anyone. Parvati's answer is the heart of the selection. She doesn't argue with the facts. She says, in effect, that the visitor doesn't know who Shiva is: what looks poor and strange from outside is exactly what she loves. And she won't sit and listen to him being insulted. She gets up to leave. Then the visitor drops the disguise. It's Shiva himself, who came to test her and found her immovable. Where Kama's arrow failed, her own tapas succeeds. Shiva agrees to marry her. Here is the teaching. Tapas isn't punishing yourself. In Hindu practice it's devotion you can see: steady effort offered to God, kept up when it's hard and when someone calls it pointless. That's why so many Hindus keep a vrata, a vow, for Shiva: a Monday fast, or the Teej fast women keep in memory of Parvati's. Small tapas, offered for love.
screen: `TAPAS: EFFORT THAT BURNS CLEAN.` · `SHE GAVE UP EVEN LEAVES.` · `THE VISITOR MOCKS SHIVA.` · `A VOW KEPT FOR LOVE.` · then, large: `DEVOTION PROVEN BY STEADY EFFORT.`

segments.voice: Pick one small vow you'll keep steady this week, the way families keep a Monday fast for Shiva: a lamp each evening, a few rounds of Om Namah Shivaya. If you don't pray, choose one steady practice of attention instead. When a voice starts in, telling you it's pointless, notice it the way Parvati noticed the visitor, and stay put.
The Shiva Purana. Today's selection: Parvati's tapas, the visitor who mocked Shiva, and the loyalty that turned out to be the test.

1122.title: The wedding of Shiva and Parvati
1122.hook: the bride's mother faints at the ash-covered groom; why Shiva, the auspicious one, and Parvati are the couple Hindu brides pray to
1122.carry: shiva means auspicious, even covered in ash
1122.tomorrow: why did the whole world become Shiva's chariot?
1122.howItsDone: The wedding of Shiva and Parvati is retold in the Shiva Purana and other Puranas and honored in temple festivals and in Kalyanasundara images; in many families a bride prays to Gauri, Parvati, before her own wedding.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Purana, Parvati won Shiva by tapas: devotion proven by steady effort. Today, the wedding.
screen: `TAPAS: DEVOTION PROVEN BY EFFORT.` · `TODAY: THE WEDDING.`

segments.voice: On the roof of the mountain king's palace, a mother waits to see her future son-in-law. Her name is Mena. Down the road comes the wedding procession, and it is splendid: gods in bright clothes, on fine mounts, with music. Each time a shining figure goes by, Mena asks, is that him? Is that Shiva? And each time she's told, no, that's one of his guests. Then the rest of the procession comes around the bend, and she gets her first look at the groom.
screen: `A MOTHER ON THE ROOF.` → `IS THAT HIM? NO, A GUEST.` → `THEN THE GROOM COMES INTO VIEW.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana's telling, Shiva's own companions, his ganas, come behind the gods. Some have strange faces, some are like ghosts and goblins, some are howling and dancing. In the middle rides Shiva on his bull, smeared with ash, snakes for ornaments, dressed like a man who lives in cremation grounds. Mena faints. When she comes to, she's furious. She blames the sage Narada, who encouraged the match, and says she'd rather see her daughter dead than married to that. She will not give her away. Parvati doesn't defend herself by pretending Shiva is ordinary. She simply says she will marry no one else. She has already chosen. The gods and sages plead with Mena. Shiva, the god who burned Kama for trying to move him, bends for his mother-in-law. He takes on a form of great beauty, adorned like a bridegroom. Mena looks again, and this time she's delighted. The wedding goes ahead, and the whole mountain celebrates. Temple art remembers that face: Shiva as the handsome groom taking Parvati's hand is called Kalyanasundara. But notice the name everyone was arguing about. Shiva means the auspicious one, the kind, the blessed. The groom in cremation ash is, by name, good fortune itself. Mena saw the ash; Parvati saw who he was. That's why Shiva and Parvati are the model couple of Hindu marriage. In many families a bride prays to Gauri, which is Parvati, before her wedding, and girls pray for a husband like Shiva; many say that means a love that sees past the ash.
screen: `THE GROOM: ASH, SNAKES, A BULL.` · `MENA FAINTS AND SAYS NO.` · `PARVATI: NO ONE ELSE.` · `SHIVA MEANS AUSPICIOUS.` · then, large: `THE MODEL COUPLE OF HINDU MARRIAGE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone your family sees only the ash of: a new partner from another background, an in-law, a neighbor whose ways are strange to you. Notice what you see first, the way Mena saw the ash. Then ask what Parvati asked: who is this, really? If you pray, hold them before Shiva and Parvati, or God, in your own words. If you don't, just hold the question.

1123.title: Tripurantaka: the three cities
1123.hook: three flying cities fall to one arrow; why Hindus light lamps on Kartik's full moon, and what Shiva the destroyer destroys
1123.carry: shiva's fire burns what binds the soul
1123.tomorrow: why is that statue half a man and half a woman?
1123.howItsDone: Shiva as Tripurantaka, the ender of the three cities, is retold in the Shiva Purana and shown in temple sculpture with his bow drawn; many Hindus remember the victory on Kartik's full moon, Tripuri Purnima, when Varanasi lines its riverbanks with lamps for Dev Deepawali.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Purana, a mother fainted at the groom, and Parvati saw who he was: Shiva means auspicious, even covered in ash. Today, three cities.
screen: `SHIVA MEANS AUSPICIOUS.` · `TODAY: THREE CITIES.`

segments.voice: Every contract has a clause somebody hopes nobody will read. Three brothers in the Shiva Purana write theirs very carefully. They are the sons of Taraka, the demon whose boon sent the gods looking for a son of Shiva. With the marriage done, that son, Kartikeya, has defeated their father. Now the brothers practice tapas in the forest until Brahma, the creator, appears and offers a boon. They ask never to die. Brahma says no. So they ask for something cleverer.
screen: `THE SONS OF TARAKA.` → `NEVER TO DIE? NO.` → `SOMETHING CLEVERER.`

segments.voice: Three cities. Maya, the great builder of the demons, makes them: one of gold in the heavens, one of silver in the sky, one of iron on the earth. And here's the clause. The cities can be destroyed only when the three come into line, which happens rarely, and only by a single arrow. Never dying, with better paperwork. The brothers flourish, then turn on the gods, and the gods come to Shiva. So the gods make him a chariot out of the world itself. The earth is the chariot, the sun and the moon its wheels. Brahma takes the reins. A mountain is the bow, and Vishnu himself becomes the arrow. When the cities slide into line, Shiva looses it, and all three burn at once. That's why he's called Tripurantaka, the ender of the three cities. The full moon of Kartik, in autumn, is called Tripuri Purnima, and in Varanasi the riverbanks are lined with lamps, Dev Deepawali, the gods' own Diwali. Then the teachers go deeper. In South Indian Shaiva teaching, going back to the poet-saint Tirumular, the three cities are read as three bonds that hold a soul: the small, grasping ego, karma, and the pull of the passing world. Read that way, Shiva's arrow isn't aimed at us, but at what traps us: the grudge that runs you, the pride you can't put down. That is what Shiva the destroyer destroys, and why teachers call his fire grace.
screen: `THREE CITIES: GOLD, SILVER, IRON.` · `THE WHOLE WORLD BECOMES THE CHARIOT.` · `KARTIK'S FULL MOON OF LAMPS.` · `THREE CITIES, THREE BONDS.` · then, large: `HIS FIRE BURNS WHAT BINDS.`

segments.voice: If you can, light a lamp or a candle, the way families do on Kartik's full moon. Name one bond you'd like loosened: a grudge, a pride, a habit that runs you. Hold it before the flame, and as the breath goes out, say Om Namah Shivaya, or the name of God you use, offering it to the fire. If you don't pray, simply watch the flame and name what you'd like to let go.

1124.title: Ardhanarishvara: the lord who is half woman
1124.hook: the creator's world won't grow until Shiva appears as half himself, half the goddess: God and God's power in one body
1124.carry: shiva and shakti are never two
1124.tomorrow: why is the dancer's face so calm?
1124.howItsDone: Ardhanarishvara, Shiva as half man and half woman, appears in temple sculpture and bronzes and is worshiped as a picture of Shiva and Shakti inseparable; Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha opens by bowing to Parvati and Shiva joined like a word and its meaning.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Purana, three cities lined up and fell to one arrow: Shiva's fire burns what binds the soul. Today, the last selection.
screen: `HIS FIRE BURNS WHAT BINDS.` · `THE LAST SELECTION.`

segments.voice: A bronze figure stands with a slight sway at the hip. On its right side: a man's flat chest, matted hair piled high, a snake for an earring. On the left: a woman's breast, smooth braided hair, a round earring, an anklet on the foot, the hip curving out. Not two figures standing close. One figure, split down the middle. This is Ardhanarishvara, and the Shiva Purana tells a story about why the creator needed to see it.
screen: `RIGHT SIDE: MATTED HAIR, A SNAKE.` → `LEFT SIDE: BRAID, EARRING, ANKLET.` → `ONE FIGURE, SPLIT DOWN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Brahma, the creator, has a problem. He makes beings from his own mind, and they don't multiply. The world stays small. So he does tapas, and Shiva appears to him in this form, half himself and half the goddess. Brahma bows and asks the goddess side for help. She gives a power of her own so that creation can go on, and in the story the world begins to grow through women and men together. So the picture isn't a riddle. It's an answer: creation doesn't go forward on one half. The name says it plainly: ardha, half, nari, woman, ishvara, lord. The lord who is half woman. Some Shaiva teachers put it this way: Shiva and Shakti, the god and his power, are never really two. One poet found an image for it. At the opening of his long poem the Raghuvamsha, Kalidasa bows to Parvati and Shiva, the parents of the world, joined, he says, like a word and its meaning. Try separating those. A word with no meaning is noise; a meaning with no word can't be said. So the teaching is plain: in Shaiva and Shakta thought, God isn't only male, and Shakti, the power that makes and moves the world, isn't a lesser half. It's God's own power. It's why, in Hindi, a wife can be called ardhangini, the half of the body, and why many rites are done by husband and wife together. That's the last selection from the Shiva Purana: Sati and Parvati, who circled Shiva through all those stories, now standing in one body with him.
screen: `BRAHMA'S WORLD WON'T GROW.` · `HALF SHIVA, HALF THE GODDESS.` · `LIKE A WORD AND ITS MEANING.` · `SHAKTI IS GOD'S OWN POWER.` · then, large: `SHIVA AND SHAKTI ARE NEVER TWO.`

segments.voice: Bring your attention to the right side of the body, the hand, the shoulder, the foot, and breathe there a few breaths; then move to the left side and breathe there. Then let the line down the middle go soft, and feel the whole body breathing as one thing. If you pray, you can say the names Shiva and Shakti, or the name of God you use, and let them rest together.

segments.voice: A woman climbs a holy mountain without once setting her feet on it; it's Shiva's home, and she goes up upside down. She is thin as a skeleton, by her own prayer: when her husband grew afraid of her devotion and left, she asked Shiva to take her beauty away. Now she's coming to Kailash. And when Shiva sees her, the story says, he turns to Parvati and says: here comes our mother. Her name is Karaikkal Ammaiyar, the mother from Karaikkal, and she has one thing to ask.
screen: `UP THE MOUNTAIN, FEET NEVER TOUCHING.` → `SHE GAVE UP HER BEAUTY.` → `HERE COMES OUR MOTHER.`

segments.voice: In the Periya Puranam, the Tamil lives of Shiva's saints, Shiva asks what she wants. In the telling, she asks not to be born again; if she must be, never to forget him; and above all, to sit at his feet and sing while he dances. He sends her south, to Tiruvalangadu, where tradition says she watches his dance forever. Her poems are among the oldest songs to Shiva the dancer, and old bronzes show her small and bony at his feet, singing. So look at what she wanted to see. Nataraja: nata, dancer, raja, king. The king of dancers. Arms swinging, hair flying, a ring of fire, one leg kicked high. And in the middle of all that motion, the face: calm, sometimes with the faintest smile. The dance is called the ananda tandava, the dance of bliss. Many Hindus read it as God moving the whole world without strain. And here's the practice it explains: darshan, seeing. When the curtain opens at a temple, people press forward not to hear a speech but to see God, and to be seen. The mother of Karaikkal gave up beauty, home and husband, and asked for darshan forever. Most of what a screen shows you is looking for your attention. Darshan turns that around: you look at the face that is already looking at you, kindly.
screen: `SHE ASKS TO WATCH HIM DANCE.` · `NATARAJA, KING OF DANCERS.` · `EVERYTHING MOVES BUT THE FACE.` · `THE DANCE OF BLISS.` · then, large: `DARSHAN: TO SEE AND BE SEEN.`

segments.voice: If you have an image of God at home, a picture or a murti, rest your eyes on its face for a few slow breaths, the way people stand at darshan. If you don't pray, look at something living instead, a plant, a tree, the sky. Let your own face go quiet like the dancer's: forehead smooth, jaw loose, eyes soft. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya, or the name of God you use, as you look.
Nataraja explained. Nataraja is the king of dancers, Shiva as lord of the dance, seen today through the eyes of the saint who asked to watch him forever.

segments.voice: Yesterday, through the eyes of Karaikkal Ammaiyar: darshan, to see God and be seen. Today, the first hand.
screen: `DARSHAN: TO SEE AND BE SEEN.` · `TODAY: THE DRUM.`

segments.voice: A street vendor in Varanasi holds up a little drum shaped like an hourglass, two small heads joined at a narrow waist, two beads hanging on cords. He twists his wrist back and forth, and the beads fly out and strike the heads, left, right, left, right, a fast rattling rhythm that carries down the lane. It's called a damaru. Look up at Nataraja's upper right hand, and there it is, held between finger and thumb.
screen: `AN HOURGLASS DRUM, TWO BEADS.` → `A TWIST OF THE WRIST.` → `THE UPPER RIGHT HAND.`

segments.voice: The drum is tied to sound, and in this tradition sound comes close to the beginning of things. Before anything is made, something is said, or struck, or sung. So the drum in Nataraja's hand is read as the beat that starts the world, the rhythm the whole dance moves to. Grammarians tell a story about it. At the end of Shiva's dance, the story goes, he sounded the damaru, and out came the sounds of the Sanskrit language, set out in short lists. Those lists are real. They sit at the head of Panini's grammar of Sanskrit, and they're called the Maheshvara Sutras, the sutras of the great lord. The very first list begins with three vowels: a, i, u. Whatever you make of the story, notice what it claims: the ordered sounds of a language, the building blocks of hymns and grocery lists alike, came from the rhythm of a dance. And behind the story is a real Hindu teaching: sound itself can be sacred. The Vedas were carried for centuries by ear, teacher to student, every syllable kept exact. The Upanishads call the syllable Om Brahman itself. So a mantra isn't only a message to God; the sound is part of the offering. That's why a grandmother corrects your Om Namah Shivaya, and why a chant in words you barely know can still fill a room. Nataraja holds that beat up where everyone can see it. The dance starts here.
screen: `THE DRUM: THE BEAT THAT STARTS IT.` · `THE SOUNDS FROM SHIVA'S DRUM.` · `A, I, U: THE FIRST LIST.` · `SOUND ITSELF IS SACRED.` · then, large: `A MANTRA IS HOLY SOUND.`

segments.voice: Say Om Namah Shivaya, Shiva's five-syllable mantra, slowly, aloud or under your breath, and let each sound land before the next: na, mah, shi, vaa, ya. Don't hurry toward the meaning; let the sound itself be the offering, the way the drum's beat comes before any word. If you don't pray, hum one long, low note and feel it in your chest, then listen to the quiet after it.
Nataraja explained. Today, the damaru, the small hourglass drum in his upper right hand: the beat that starts the dance, and in the grammarians' story, the source of the sounds of Sanskrit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nataraja's drum: a mantra is holy sound, not just meaning. Today, the other hand, and the end of a week.
screen: `A MANTRA IS HOLY SOUND.` · `TODAY: THE FLAME.`

segments.voice: In Varanasi, which Hindus also call Kashi, there's a cremation ground on the bank of the Ganga called Manikarnika. People say its fires haven't gone out in centuries. Families carry their dead down the steps, day and night. And tradition tells something remarkable about this place: here, Shiva himself bends to the ear of each person who dies, and whispers the mantra of crossing over, and they are set free. Now look at Nataraja. Opposite the drum, in his upper left hand, held in an open palm, is a flame.
screen: `MANIKARNIKA: THE FIRES NEVER OUT.` → `SHIVA WHISPERS TO THE DYING.` → `A FLAME IN THE UPPER LEFT HAND.`

segments.voice: In the usual reading of the image, the flame is samhara, dissolution. Things are made, last a while, and are drawn back in. Look where the classic bronzes put it: drum on one side, flame on the other, both at the same height, neither higher, neither dropped. The beginning in one hand, the ending in the other. That's a big Hindu teaching. Time turns in great cycles; the Puranas say that at the end of a great cycle the worlds are drawn back in, and in time made again. And the ending is as much God's work as the beginning. So Shiva's fire isn't the enemy of life. In Kashi, it's where freedom is whispered. And remember who holds it: the groom smeared with ash, the god of the cremation ground. That's why many Shaiva Hindus wear vibhuti, sacred ash, often in three lines across the forehead. Many read it this way: everything burns down to this, and Shiva wears it like clothing, because what he is can't burn. And families still carry a loved one's ashes to the Ganga, many to Kashi itself. Then the week, looked back on: Parvati's tapas, a wedding, three cities, the lord who is half woman, a saint at the dancer's feet, the drum, and now the flame. A grandmother dies, a job ends, a childhood home is sold. The flame in Nataraja's hand says the ending is held too, by the same hand that keeps the beat.
screen: `THE FLAME: SAMHARA, THE ENDING.` · `DRUM AND FLAME AT THE SAME HEIGHT.` · `VIBHUTI: THE ASH SHIVA WEARS.` · `A WEEK, LOOKED BACK ON.` · then, large: `THE ENDING IS GOD'S WORK TOO.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up: into the right palm put something beginning in your life, and into the left something that's ending, or needs to. Let both hands rest at the same height and breathe with both. If you keep vibhuti, you can touch a little to your forehead; if you pray, offer both hands to Shiva, or to God, with Om Namah Shivaya. If you don't pray, simply hold both, level.
Nataraja explained. Today, the flame in his upper left hand: samhara, the ending, held level with the drum's beginning, both part of the same dance.
